e-12763.knowledge_point: Finding Unions and Intersections of Finite Families of Indexed Sets
e-12763.problem: Find $\,\displaystyle \bigcup_{i \in I} S_i$, given that $I = \{ -1, 0, 1 \},$ and $S_i = (i-1, \,i+1).$
e-12763.worked_solution:
The union of a family of indexed sets is the set containing all elements belonging to *at least one* set in the indexed family:

$$
\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i = \big\{ x\in U \: : \: x \in A_i \:\:\textrm{for at least one } A_i,\:\: i \in I \big\}
$$

where $U$ is a universal set.

Therefore, in our case, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{⋃}_{i\in I}{S}_{i} & ={S}_{-1}\cup {S}_{0}\cup {S}_{1} \\  & =(-2,0)\,\cup \,(-1,1)\,\cup \,(0,2) \\  & =(-2,2).\end{aligned}
$$

e-12764.knowledge_point: Finding Unions and Intersections of (Countably) Infinite Families of Indexed Sets
e-12764.problem: Find $\,\displaystyle \bigcap_{i \in I} X_i$  given that $I = \mathbb{N}$ and $X_i = \{ i, \, 2i \}.$
e-12764.worked_solution:
The intersection of a family of indexed sets $\{A_i\}_{i\in I}$ contains all elements that belong to *all* sets in our family:

$$
\bigcap_{i \in I} A_i = \big\{ x\in U \: : \: x \in A_i \:\:\textrm{for all } A_i,\:\: i \in I \big\}
$$

where $U$ is a universal set.

Let's now write down a few instances of our indexed sets:

- if $i=1,$ we have $X_1 = \{ 1, 2 \}$

- if $i=2,$ we have $X_2 = \{ 2, 4 \}$

- if $i=3,$ we have $X_3 = \{ 3, 6 \}$

- if $i=4,$ we have $X_4 = \{ 4, 8 \}$

and so on. 

Notice that there is no element that belongs to all the sets. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{⋂}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}=∅.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The union contains every element in at least one of the three sets. Combining their elements gives {−2,−1,0,1,2}.

after.name: Question 6
after.worked_solution:
The union of a family of indexed sets is the set containing all elements belonging to *at least one* set in the indexed family:

$$
{⋃}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}={x\in U\,:\,x\in {A}_{i}\,\,\text{for at least one }{A}_{i},\,\,i\in I}
$$

where $U$ is a universal set.

Therefore, in our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{⋃}_{i\in I}{X}_{i} & ={X}_{-2}\cup {X}_{1}\cup {X}_{2} \\  & ={-2,-1,0}\,\cup \,{0,1}\,\cup \,{0,1,2} \\  & ={-2,-1,0,1,2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The union of a family of indexed sets is the set containing all elements belonging to *at least one* set in the indexed family:

$$
{⋃}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}={x\in U\,:\,x\in {A}_{i}\,\,\text{for at least one }{A}_{i},\,\,i\in I}
$$

where $U$ is a universal set.

Therefore, in our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{⋃}_{i\in I}{X}_{i} & ={X}_{3}\cup {X}_{5}\cup {X}_{7} \\  & ={-3,0,3}\,\cup \,{3,5}\,\cup \,{-7,0,3} \\  & ={-7,-3,0,3,5}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 11
after.worked_solution:
The intersection of a family of indexed sets ${{A}_{i}}_{i\in I}$ contains all elements that belong to *all* sets in our family:

$$
{⋂}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}={x\in U\,:\,x\in {A}_{i}\,\,\text{for all }{A}_{i},\,\,i\in I}
$$

where $U$ is a universal set.

Let's now write down a few instances of our indexed sets:

- if $i=-1,$ we have ${X}_{-1}={-2,-1}$

- if $i=0,$ we have ${X}_{0}={-1,0}$

- if $i=1,$ we have ${X}_{1}={0,1}$

and so on. 

Notice that there is no element that belongs to all the sets. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{⋂}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}=∅.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 12
after.worked_solution:
The union of a family of indexed sets is the set containing all elements belonging to *at least one* set in the indexed family:

$$
{⋃}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}={x\in U\,:\,x\in {A}_{i}\,\,\text{for at least one }{A}_{i},\,\,i\in I}
$$

where $U$ is a universal set.

The notation ${⋃}_{i=3}^{\infty }$ means that our set of indexes is 
${3,4,5…}.$ 

Let's now write down a few instances of our indexed sets:

- if $i=3,$ we have ${S}_{3}=[\frac{1}{3},1]$

- if $i=4,$ we have ${S}_{4}=[\frac{1}{4},1]$

- if $i=5,$ we have ${S}_{5}=[\frac{1}{5},1]$

- $⋯$

and so on. 

Notice that as $i$ increases, 

- the left endpoint of the intervals approaches $0$ but never reaches it, and

- the right endpoint of the intervals equals $1$ for all the sets.

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{⋃}_{i=3}^{\infty }{S}_{i}=(0,1].\end{aligned}
$$

The union of a family of indexed sets is the set containing all elements belonging to at least one set in the indexed family:

⋃i∈IAi={x∈U:x∈Aifor at least one Ai,i∈I} where U is a universal set.

after.name: Question 14
after.worked_solution:
The union of a family of indexed sets is the set containing all elements belonging to *at least one* set in the indexed family:

$$
{⋃}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}={x\in U\,:\,x\in {A}_{i}\,\,\text{for at least one }{A}_{i},\,\,i\in I}
$$

where $U$ is a universal set.

The notation ${⋃}_{i=5}^{\infty }$ means that our set of indexes is 
${5,6,7…}.$ 

Let's now write down a few instances of our indexed sets:

- if $i=5,$ we have ${S}_{5}=[1+\frac{1}{5},2]=[\frac{6}{5},2]$

- if $i=6,$ we have ${S}_{6}=[1+\frac{1}{6},2]=[\frac{7}{6},2]$

- if $i=7,$ we have ${S}_{7}=[1+\frac{1}{7},2]=[\frac{8}{7},2]$

- $⋯$

and so on. 

Notice that as $i$ increases, 

- the left endpoint of the intervals approaches $1$ but never reaches it, and

- the right endpoint of the intervals equals $2$ for all the sets.

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{⋃}_{i=5}^{\infty }{S}_{i}=(1,2].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 15
after.worked_solution:
The intersection of a family of indexed sets ${{A}_{i}}_{i\in I}$ contains all elements that belong to *all* sets in our family:

$$
{⋂}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}={x\in U\,:\,x\in {A}_{i}\,\,\text{for all }{A}_{i},\,\,i\in I}
$$

where $U$ is a universal set.

The notation ${⋂}_{i=1}^{\infty }$ means that index set is 
$N={1,2,3…}.$ 

Let's now write down a few instances of our indexed sets:

- if $i=1,$ we have ${X}_{1}={0,1,2}$

- if $i=2,$ we have ${X}_{2}={0,2,4}$

- if $i=3,$ we have ${X}_{3}={0,3,6}$

- $⋯$

and so on. 

Notice that the only element that lies in all the sets is $0.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{⋂}_{i=1}^{\infty }{X}_{i}={0}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The intersection of a family of indexed sets {Ai}i∈I contains all elements that belong to all sets in our family:

⋂i∈IAi={x∈U:x∈Aifor all Ai,i∈I} where U is a universal set.

The notation ⋂i=1∞ means that index set is N={1,2,3…}.

Let's now write down a few instances of our indexed sets:

  • if i=1, we have X1={0,1,2}

  • if i=2, we have X2={0,2,4}

  • if i=3, we have X3={0,3,6}

  • ⋯

and so on.

Notice that the only element that lies in all the sets is 0. Therefore,

⋂i=1∞Xi={0}.

$$
{⋂}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}={x\in U\,:\,x\in {A}_{i}\,\,\text{for all }{A}_{i},\,\,i\in I}
$$

where $U$ is a universal set.

The notation ${⋂}_{i=1}^{\infty }$ means that index set is 
$N={1,2,3…}.$ 

Let's now write down a few instances of our indexed sets:

- if $i=1,$ we have ${X}_{1}={0,1,2}$

- if $i=2,$ we have ${X}_{2}={0,2,4}$

- if $i=3,$ we have ${X}_{3}={0,3,6}$

- $⋯$

and so on. 

Notice that the only element that lies in all the sets is $0.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{⋂}_{i=1}^{\infty }{X}_{i}={0}.\end{aligned}
$$
